eyebrow: Python for Data Engineers · Chapter 3, Lesson 13
subtitle: Opening files the right way — and why with matters.

code:
with open("orders.csv", "r") as f:
    header = f.readline()
    first_row = f.readline()

print(header)
print(first_row)
caption: with closes the file automatically the moment you leave it — even if an exception happens inside.

eyebrow: readlines() vs. iterating line by line
code:
with open("orders.csv") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()
print(len(lines))

# Better for large files -- one line at a time:
with open("orders.csv") as f:
    next(f)  # skip the header
    for line in f:
        fields = line.strip().split(",")
        print(fields[0], fields[2])
caption: readlines() loads every line into memory at once; iterating the file object doesn't.

code:
# Works here, because no field contains a comma...
fields = line.strip().split(",")

# ...but a product name like "Tent, 2-Person" would
# split into two fields and shift every column after
# it out of alignment.
caption: Real CSVs quote fields with embedded commas — a plain split can't tell the difference.

code:
with open("orders_summary.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write(f"Shipped orders: {shipped_count}\n")
    f.write("Generated by Lesson 13 script\n")

with open("orders_summary.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("Re-run confirmed.\n")
caption: "w" overwrites the whole file every run; "a" appends to what's already there.
